claims.text: In CoCrFeMnNi, chemical short-range order modulates the local energy landscape experienced by dislocations.
The degree of short-range order governs the yield strength of CoCrFeMnNi.
The degree of short-range order governs the strain-hardening behavior of CoCrFeMnNi.
The degree of short-range order governs the overall deformation performance of CoCrFeMnNi.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi material is single-phase and chemically homogeneous.
Rapid quenching from high temperature produces a chemically disordered CoCrFeMnNi state.
Annealing CoCrFeMnNi at 700°C for 1–10 hours promotes the development of short-range order.
Rapid quenching freezes CoCrFeMnNi in a disordered state with minimal short-range order.
Diffuse scattering, atom probe tomography, and electron nanodiffraction can characterize the degree and spatial extent of short-range order.
Increased short-range order creates locally varying bonding environments.
The local environments created by short-range order modify the energy barriers encountered by moving dislocations.
Short-range-order-induced local fluctuations act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
These obstacles enhance yield strength relative to a disordered matrix.
These obstacles influence strain-hardening behavior relative to a disordered matrix.
Annealed CoCrFeMnNi samples with enhanced short-range order will have higher yield strength than quenched samples.
Annealed CoCrFeMnNi samples with enhanced short-range order will have an altered strain-hardening rate relative to quenched samples.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for CoCrFeMnNi under the specified thermal treatments and room-temperature testing.
A lack of a systematic, statistically significant relationship between quantified short-range order and mechanical performance relative to the quenched control would falsify the hypothesis.
